This article describes how GiottoLens works and why, for contributors and advanced users.
Decisions with a recorded argument link to their ADR in `adr/`; numbers are from the Atera
example (170k cells, about 600M transcripts in 853 tiles) in headless Chrome.

## Goals

1. Full-resolution exploration of GiottoDisk-backed data at any size.
2. Reactive pan, zoom and selection.
3. Selections and annotations that come back to R, as cell IDs or Giotto objects.
4. Panels drawn from the same GiottoVisuals specs as static figures.
5. Fully drivable from R, so an agent working in the user's R session can read and steer the
   viewer without seeing it.

GiottoLens always runs with an R session alongside it. The data model and data operations
belong to the giotto object and GiottoClass/GiottoDisk; the browser draws what R prepares and
keeps no second model of its own (adr/0003). Anything that would work the same on any table,
with no giotto object behind it, belongs in dbVisuals instead.

## Overview

```
R session                                   Browser
launch_lens()                               deck.gl (OrthographicView, Y up)
  httpuv on 127.0.0.1:<random port>          zustand store: config + selection rules
    /lens/           viewer bundle           rules -> masks over all cells (typed arrays)
    /lens/session/   manifest, cells,        hyparquet + own point decoder (workers)
                     metadata, panel data    Vega-Lite panels (loaded on demand)
    /lens/files/     tile stores, whole
    /lens/data/      tile stores, by Range
    WebSocket (token) <-------------------->  requests, selections, rules, logs, errors
```

## Serving

`launch_lens()` serves everything from one httpuv server so the IDE viewer panes (Positron,
RStudio) can reach the WebSocket on the same origin. Nothing is copied or written next to
the data: the viewer bundle is served from the installed package, each GiottoDisk tile store
is mounted in place, and per-viewer files (manifest, `cells.parquet`, pushed metadata and panel
data) go to a temp directory removed by `close()`.

Every URL sits under `/lens/` and the viewer resolves them against the page, so a proxy that
adds a path prefix (RStudio Server, Workbench, a port forward) forwards one unit.

The server binds `127.0.0.1` on a random port. The WebSocket needs a per-launch token carried
in the viewer URL; an Origin check additionally rejects foreign pages, except behind RStudio
Server's proxy, where the Origin is the proxy's and the token alone decides (adr/0006).

## Cells

The viewer numbers cells by concatenating the polygon tiles in manifest order: tile `t` holds
cells `offset[t] .. offset[t] + n[t] - 1`. R builds this table once at launch
(`cells.parquet`: centroid x, y and the ID) and keeps the IDs; the browser loads the centroids
into two `Float32Array`s and never needs a string ID (adr/0002). Consequences:

- A polygon tile row maps to its cell by addition, so colouring and selection highlighting
  of outlines need no lookup.
- All cells are drawn as centroids from the start, whatever is loaded: all 170k Atera cells
  appear in 0.12–0.16 s. Polygon tiles are only fetched for outlines, near outline zoom.
- Metadata pushed with `push_metadata()` is written in the same order, one typed array per
  column (categories as integer codes with their levels), so the browser joins nothing.
- Selections cross the socket as bitmasks over this order: N/8 bytes whatever is selected.

## Selection rules

A selection is one **rule** per source: the spatial view (lasso, brush), the scatter, each
histogram, the metadata filter, pushed panels and R. Rule kinds: `polygon`, `stroke`,
`range`, `categories`, `compare`, `ids` and `union`, each optionally negated. Sources combine
with OR, or with AND in cross-filter mode, where each panel shows the other sources only.

Rules, not cell lists, are the state (adr/0001):

- They evaluate to masks over **all** cells, so a lasso drawn zoomed out over unloaded
  tiles selects what the same lasso selects zoomed in.
- They are evaluated the same way in the browser (`selection/rules.ts`) and in R
  (`R/rules.R`). `viewer$select()` resolves cells with no browser open, and a rule read back
  from the browser gives the same cells in R. The end-to-end tests compare the two.
- They describe themselves: `viewer$rules()` lists each with a summary and its own cell count,
  `viewer$rules(code = TRUE)` prints the `lens_*()` calls that recreate the selection, and the
  rules strip shows them in the viewer.

Evaluation stays interactive at scale. A point-in-polygon test with edges bucketed into
horizontal bands (`ringTester()`) runs a whole-view lasso over 10M cells in 248 ms (a plain
edge loop took 1.5 s) and is nearly flat in vertex count; tile bounds prune the cells tested.
Masks are cached per rule object, brushes build theirs incrementally while dragging, and
range, category and AND/OR steps are single passes (a cross-filter step on Atera: 2.8 ms).
Up to roughly 10–20M cells the browser holds everything it needs; beyond that, the plan is
R-side evaluation (see the roadmap).

## Browser state and rendering

Configuration (layers, colouring, rules, combine mode, annotations, tool settings) lives in
a zustand store and changes only through its actions; it can be saved as JSON. Runtime data
(deck instance, caches, loaded tables, in-progress drawing) is kept apart. Every store change
requests a render, batched to one per animation frame.

deck.gl compares `data` by reference, so binary data objects are built once per underlying
array. Rebuilding them each render had deck re-triangulate every polygon tile and re-upload
every buffer on each tile arrival: 1.3–1.5 s of main-thread blocking while loading, down to
about 90 ms with the objects reused.

## Reading tiles

Parquet stores each column of each row group as its own block, so reading a few columns of a
tile means one byte range per column per row group. How tiles are fetched therefore depends
on where the browser is (adr/0004):

- **whole**: one request per tile from httpuv's own thread, with no R involved. On the same
  machine the extra bytes cost nothing and a busy R does not stall panning (10 tiles and
  outlines: 0.9 s, R free or busy).
- **columns**: the footer, then only the needed blocks, merged when less than 1 MB apart
  (about two requests per tile), through the Range handler on R's main thread. About 6x fewer
  bytes, for slow links; while R is busy these requests wait.
- **auto** (default) starts with whole tiles on a localhost URL and switches to columns after
  two slow whole fetches, since an SSH port forward also looks like localhost.

Transcript tiles decode in a pool of Web Workers with GiottoLens' own decoder for the three
drawn columns (adr/0005). It reads dictionary-encoded columns as integer indices, looks up
only the rows the zoom tier keeps (every 16th, 4th or all) and maps gene names to gene
indices once per dictionary entry: 2.6x faster than hyparquet for all rows and 3.4x at 1/16,
with identical output. Layouts it does not cover fall back to hyparquet. Codecs: SNAPPY (WASM),
ZSTD, GZIP, LZ4_RAW and Hadoop LZ4.

At zoomed-out views loading is now bound by bytes, not decoding, which is what the planned
coarse tier addresses.

## The R API is the agent API

Every user action has an R equivalent on the `LensViewer` object, so an agent in the user's R
session can work with the viewer as well as the user can: read it (`describe()`, `state()`,
`rules()`, `log()`, `screenshot()`), drive it (`select()`, `set_view()`, `zoom_to()`,
`color_by()`, `set_layer()`, `push_panel()`), ask the user for input
(`wait_for_selection()`) and get results back as R objects (`selection`, `subset()`).

The protocol is request/reply: a message from R with an `id` is answered by the browser with
the handler's result or error. A tab announces `ready` once its handlers are registered, and
R then sends it the current metadata and rules, so reloads and new tabs match. Browser errors
are forwarded and printed in the R console.

## Panels

The stats column holds a scatter of any two metadata columns and a histogram or bar chart,
both drawn from the typed arrays and linked by the selection rules. `push_panel()` adds any
Vega-Lite spec, including GiottoVisuals' `renderSpec(engine = "vegalite")`; rows with a
`cell_ID` are linked, and an interval brush named `brush` becomes a selection rule. Mosaic is
not used: linking comes from the rules, and aggregation from typed-array scans (about 1 ms per
million cells) or from R.

## The large-data path

Selections over cells stay in the browser up to about 10–20M cells. Beyond that, and for
queries over transcripts, the work belongs in R next to the files. Bare SQL on the parquet
tiles sets the floor (one 200-vertex lasso, cell IDs returned to R):

| Data | DuckDB (8 threads) | DuckDB (1 thread) | sedona |
|---|---|---|---|
| 170k cells, centroid | 16 ms | 30 ms | 6 ms |
| 170k cells, geometry intersects | 36 ms | 129 ms | 54 ms |
| transcripts, 420M in the lasso | 49 s | 101 s | 5.3 s |
| transcripts, 1.1M in the lasso | 0.53 s | 0.81 s | 0.83 s |

GiottoDisk's `spatRelate()` took 1.4 s (sedona), 1.8 s (terra) and 5.7 s (duckdb) for the
same cell lasso: per-call overhead, not engine time (adr/0007). At transcript scale nothing
returns IDs interactively, so the server path serves aggregates (counts per gene, densities)
and keeps selections as rules.
